ja.description: LNA・ミキサ・IFアンプのような3段の受信機について、各段の利得・雑音指数・IIP3から、フリスの公式で全体の雑音指数と雑音温度、総合利得、入力換算のIIP3を計算し、帯域幅と必要なSNRから受信感度を求めます。
ja.h1: 雑音指数のカスケード計算ツール
ja.lead: 受信機の各段の利得・雑音指数(NF)・IIP3を入れると、全体の性能を計算します。既定値は、LNA(利得15 dB、NF 1.5 dB)、ミキサ(変換損失7 dB、NF 7 dB)、IFアンプ(利得20 dB、NF 5 dB)の3段で、帯域幅20 MHz、必要なSNR 10 dBの場合です。使わない段は、利得0 dB・NF 0 dB・IIP3を大きな値(99 dBmなど)にしてください。
ja.in_heading: 入力(1段目がアンテナ側)
ja.sens_heading: 受信感度の目安(基準温度290 K)
ja.note: 各段のインピーダンスが整合していると仮定しています。損失のある受動素子(ケーブル・フィルタ・ミキサの変換損失)は、利得を負の値、NFを損失のdB値にして入れます。IIP3の合成は、各段のひずみが同じ位相で足し合わされる最悪の場合の近似です。

sections.h: 雑音指数とフリスの公式
sections.p: 雑音指数(NF)は、信号が回路を通るときにSNRがどれだけ悪くなるかを表す値で、雑音因子F(雑音指数の真数)を10·log10(F)でdBにしたものです。多段の回路の全体の雑音指数は、真数で F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1·G2) + … と表されます(フリスの公式)。2段目以降の雑音は、前段までの利得で割られて小さくなるので、1段目の雑音指数と利得が全体をほぼ決めます。既定値では全体のNFは約2.75 dBで、LNAの1.5 dBにミキサ以降の影響が少し加わった値になります。
受信機の先頭に低雑音増幅器(LNA)を置くのは、フリスの公式で後段の雑音を小さくするためです。逆にアンテナとLNAのあいだにケーブルやフィルタの損失があると、その損失のdB値がそのままNFに加わります。たとえば損失2 dBのケーブルのあとにNF 1.5 dBのLNAを置くと、全体のNFは約3.5 dBになります。感度が重要な受信機では、LNAをアンテナの直近に置きます。

抵抗の熱雑音の電力は kTB で、基準温度290 Kでは1 Hzあたり約 −174 dBm です。受信機の入力換算の雑音電力は −174 + 10·log10(B) + NF [dBm] となり、これに復調に必要なSNRを足したものが受信感度の目安です。既定値の帯域幅20 MHz(73 dB)、NF約2.75 dB、SNR 10 dBでは、雑音電力は約 −98.2 dBm、感度は約 −88.2 dBm です。帯域幅を半分にすると感度は約3 dB良くなります。

3次インターセプトポイント(IP3)は、3次の相互変調ひずみの大きさを表す直線性の指標です。入力換算のIIP3は、mWの真数で 1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G1/IIP3₂ + G1G2/IIP3₃ + … と合成され、後段ほど前段までの利得をかけた分だけ厳しくなります。雑音とは逆に、前段の利得が大きいほど後段の直線性が全体を悪くします。既定値では入力換算IIP3が約 −1.26 dBm で、低雑音と高い直線性のバランスをとるのが受信機の設計の要点です。

faq.q: 雑音指数と雑音温度の関係は?
faq.a: 等価雑音温度は Te = 290·(F − 1) [K] で、Fは雑音因子(雑音指数の真数)です。NF 3 dB(F ≈ 2)は約290 K、NF 1 dBは約75 Kです。衛星通信のように非常に低い雑音を扱う分野では、雑音温度で表すことが多くなります。

faq.q: 受動素子の雑音指数は?
faq.a: 周囲温度が290 Kのとき、損失L(dB)の受動素子の雑音指数はL(dB)に等しくなります。損失3 dBのフィルタはNF 3 dB、利得 −3 dBとして入れます。

faq.q: −174 dBm/Hz はどこから来ますか?
faq.a: 熱雑音の電力 kTB で、k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K、T = 290 K、B = 1 Hz とすると約4.0 × 10⁻²¹ W、つまり約 −174 dBm です。

en.card: Calculate cascaded noise figure, gain, IIP3 and receiver sensitivity with the Friis formula
en.title: Cascaded Noise Figure (NF) Calculator: Friis Formula, IIP3 and Receiver Sensitivity
en.description: For a three-stage receiver such as LNA, mixer and IF amplifier, calculate the overall noise figure and noise temperature, total gain and input-referred IIP3 from each stage's gain, noise figure and IIP3 using the Friis formula, and find the receiver sensitivity from the bandwidth and required SNR.
en.lead: Enter the gain, noise figure (NF) and IIP3 of each receiver stage to calculate the performance of the whole chain. The defaults are three stages — an LNA (15 dB gain, 1.5 dB NF), a mixer (7 dB conversion loss, 7 dB NF) and an IF amplifier (20 dB gain, 5 dB NF) — with a 20 MHz bandwidth and a required SNR of 10 dB. For an unused stage, set the gain to 0 dB, the NF to 0 dB and the IIP3 to a large value (such as 99 dBm).
en.in_heading: Inputs (stage 1 is on the antenna side)
en.note: Each stage is assumed to be impedance-matched. Enter lossy passive components (cables, filters, mixer conversion loss) with a negative gain and an NF equal to the loss in dB. The IIP3 combination is an approximation for the worst case, in which the distortion from each stage adds in phase.

sections.h: Noise figure and the Friis formula
sections.p: Noise figure (NF) expresses how much the SNR worsens as a signal passes through a circuit; it is the noise factor F (a linear value) converted to dB as 10·log10(F). The overall noise factor of a multistage circuit is F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1·G2) + … in linear terms (the Friis formula). Noise from the second stage onward is divided by the gain of the preceding stages and becomes small, so the noise figure and gain of the first stage largely set the total. With the defaults, the overall NF is about 2.75 dB: the LNA's 1.5 dB plus a small contribution from the mixer and later stages.

A low-noise amplifier (LNA) is placed at the front of a receiver so that, by the Friis formula, it makes the noise of later stages small. Conversely, any cable or filter loss between the antenna and the LNA adds its dB value directly to the NF. For example, placing an LNA with a 1.5 dB NF after a cable with 2 dB of loss gives an overall NF of about 3.5 dB. In receivers where sensitivity matters, the LNA is placed right at the antenna.

The thermal noise power of a resistor is kTB, about −174 dBm per hertz at the reference temperature of 290 K. The receiver's input-referred noise power is −174 + 10·log10(B) + NF [dBm], and adding the SNR needed for demodulation gives an estimate of the receiver sensitivity. With the default 20 MHz bandwidth (73 dB), an NF of about 2.75 dB and an SNR of 10 dB, the noise power is about −98.2 dBm and the sensitivity about −88.2 dBm. Halving the bandwidth improves the sensitivity by about 3 dB.

The third-order intercept point (IP3) is a measure of linearity that expresses the size of third-order intermodulation distortion. The input-referred IIP3 combines, in linear mW, as 1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G1/IIP3₂ + G1G2/IIP3₃ + …, so later stages become more demanding by the gain ahead of them. Opposite to noise, the higher the gain of earlier stages, the more the linearity of later stages degrades the total. With the defaults, the input-referred IIP3 is about −1.26 dBm; balancing low noise against high linearity is the key to receiver design.

faq.q: How are noise figure and noise temperature related?
faq.a: The equivalent noise temperature is Te = 290·(F − 1) [K], where F is the noise factor (the noise figure as a linear value). An NF of 3 dB (F ≈ 2) is about 290 K, and an NF of 1 dB about 75 K. In fields that deal with very low noise, such as satellite communications, noise temperature is used more often.

faq.q: What is the noise figure of a passive component?
faq.a: At an ambient temperature of 290 K, a passive component with a loss of L (dB) has a noise figure equal to L (dB). Enter a filter with 3 dB of loss as an NF of 3 dB and a gain of −3 dB.
It is the thermal noise power kTB: with k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T = 290 K and B = 1 Hz, it is about 4.0 × 10⁻²¹ W, or about −174 dBm.
